Then he began, slowly and with obvious pleasure, to count aloud, while the whole theatre held its breath.

The theatre divided at once into two roaring camps, one that cheered Cyrano for his impudence and one that howled for the play to go on. The marquises on the benches waved their lace handkerchiefs and called for the actor to continue, and the poor fellow, who had no wish at all to be skewered, stood rooted to the spot with sweat running down his cheeks. He looked first at Cyrano, then at the crowd, and then at the ceiling, as if the answer might be written there.

Cyrano swept his glance around the hall and promised in a cheerful roar that he would cut off the ears of any man who disliked his order, and then he would cut off the rest of him as well. He turned slowly on his chair, giving everyone a fair chance to accept the challenge, and the silence that followed was the loudest sound of the evening. Montfleury, who had been waiting for just such a pause, gathered up his robe and ran headlong from the stage.

Bellerose, the harassed manager of the theatre, hurried forward wringing his hands and lamenting that the evening was ruined and that the public would demand its money back. Cyrano listened with grave courtesy, then flung him a heavy purse of gold that was clearly worth far more than a night's takings. The crowd, which loved nothing so much as a magnificent gesture, roared its approval, and the manager caught the purse with a bow that was almost a prayer.

A curious young marquis leaned forward and asked Cyrano what the poor actor had done to deserve such a tongue-lashing. Cyrano replied that he had two reasons, the first being that Montfleury was a dreadful performer who murdered verse as other men murdered time. The second reason, he added with a sudden shadow in his face, was a private one that he would not give to any man in the theatre.

The Vicomte de Valvert, who was eager to please his master the Comte, strolled forward with a lazy sneer and remarked that Cyrano's nose was a very large one. There was a gasp from the crowd, for no one in Paris had ever said such a thing to Cyrano's face and lived to repeat it. Cyrano merely bowed, with a politeness that was more alarming than any anger, and agreed that it was indeed very large.

Cyrano asked, with an air of weary disappointment, whether that was really the best the Vicomte could do, for a man of wit could have found a hundred better things to say. He offered a few examples, beginning with the fierce kind, in which a man declares that he would cut off such a nose at once rather than carry it about the world. The crowd listened with delight, for it was plain that Cyrano was only warming up.

Cyrano went on, in a gentler voice, to show how a friendly man might ask whether the nose needed a hat, and how a curious man might wonder what it was used for. Each remark was cleverer than the one before, and the crowd laughed until the candles trembled. The Vicomte stood scarlet and speechless in the middle of the circle, wishing that the floor would open and swallow him.

Cyrano concluded that the Vicomte had neither wit nor manners, and that he had only dared to mock the nose because he supposed that nobody would answer him. Then, with a bow that swept his hat to the floor, he offered the gentleman a duel in which he would compose a ballad while they fought. At the last line of the poem, he promised, he would touch his opponent.

The crowd pressed back in a great circle, climbing on benches and on one another's shoulders to see, while Cyrano flung off his cloak and tossed his hat to the floor with a flourish. He announced the title of his ballad, which was to be called the duel at the Hôtel de Bourgogne, and asked the Vicomte politely to draw. Valvert, pale with fury, had no choice, and the blade rang free of its scabbard.

The two blades touched, and Cyrano began his poem at once in a clear, cheerful voice, setting each line to the rhythm of the steel as though he were taking a stroll in a garden. He rhymed as he parried and parried as he rhymed, and the crowd, hardly daring to breathe, noticed that he did not even look at his opponent's point. Poetry and swordsmanship seemed in him to be one and the same art, practised with the same easy grace.

Valvert lunged and slashed with all the fury he could muster, but his point met only empty air or the polished steel of Cyrano's blade. Each time Cyrano turned the stroke aside with an easy flick of the wrist, he praised the manner of it in his verse, and the crowd howled with laughter at the gentleman's growing despair. Not one rhyme was lost, and not one beat of the rhythm was disturbed.

In her box above the pit, Roxane leaned forward with shining eyes, quite forgetting to hide her delight at the spectacle. Christian, standing below, was watching her face more closely than the fight, and he saw with a pang how bright it had grown. On the stage the Comte de Guiche was frowning, for it was his friend who was being made to look a fool before the most beautiful woman in Paris.

As the poem neared its end, Cyrano courteously warned the sweating Vicomte that the last line was almost upon him, and that at the very moment it was spoken, the point of his sword would find its target. He even described the exact place, so that the poor gentleman might have time to prepare himself. Valvert, who could think of nothing but his own safety, heard this prophecy with terror and defended himself harder than ever.

Cyrano spoke the final line in a ringing voice, and at the final word his blade slid past the Vicomte's guard and struck exactly as he had promised. Valvert staggered, dropped his weapon, and fell into the arms of his friends, wounded but not seriously hurt. The theatre exploded in a storm of cheers, and even those who had called for the play to go on found that they were stamping their feet with the rest.

The crowd shouted Cyrano's name until the rafters rang, and he bowed to the left and to the right with the easy grace of an actor who has played his part to perfection. The Comte de Guiche rose stiffly and left the stage in a cold rage, while the wounded Vicomte was carried away by his friends with a handkerchief pressed to his side. High above them, the box where Roxane had been sitting was suddenly empty, and Christian was staring at it.

When the last of the spectators had drifted out into the night, Le Bret, who had loved Cyrano for years and worried about him every day of them, came forward with a troubled face. He praised the duel as the finest he had ever seen, but he scolded his friend sharply for making so many powerful enemies in a single evening. There was the Comte, the Vicomte, the patrons of Montfleury, and half the marquises of Paris.

Cyrano replied that he would rather have a hundred enemies and his freedom than a single powerful friend who expected him to bow. He had no wish to be anyone's pet, no wish to crawl up the ladder of fortune, and no wish to write a single verse that another man had paid for. If he must walk alone, he said, at least every step would be his own.

Le Bret asked at last for the second reason, the private one, and Cyrano's face changed so that his friend hardly knew him. In a low, unsteady voice he admitted that he had loved his cousin Roxane for years, and that the fat actor's eyes on her had been more than he could bear. It was the first time that he had said the words aloud to any living soul.

Le Bret asked why in the world Cyrano did not simply tell her, and Cyrano answered by laying a finger on his great nose with a crooked smile. He said that he could joke about it before a thousand people, but that no woman, and least of all the loveliest one in Paris, could ever look at such a face without laughter. It was the only battle in which he had never dared to draw his sword.

Le Bret pointed out that Roxane had watched the duel with shining eyes and had seemed more delighted than any woman in the theatre. Cyrano only shrugged and said that every woman loved a display of courage, and that the same smile would have been given to any fool with a sword. He refused to let himself hope, for hope, he said, was the one weapon that could really wound him.

While the two friends were talking, the door of the theatre creaked, and a stout old woman peered in with a shawl wrapped around her head. It was the Duenna, Roxane's faithful servant, and she asked in a whisper whether she might have a word with Monsieur de Bergerac. Cyrano, who had faced a hundred sword points without a tremor, felt his heart give a sudden jump.

The Duenna delivered her message with great importance: her mistress wished to see her cousin in private on the following morning and had something to tell him. Cyrano could hardly speak for astonishment, but at last he stammered out that the pastry shop of his friend Ragueneau would be a quiet place, and that he would be there at the first hour. The old woman nodded graciously, gathered her shawl about her shoulders, and went off down the street in a rustle of skirts.

As soon as the door closed, Cyrano seized Le Bret by both shoulders and danced him around the empty hall, laughing like a schoolboy let out of class. He cried that with this news in his heart he would gladly fight an army, a company of giants, or, if the world could provide them, a hundred men at once. Le Bret, laughing in spite of himself, begged him to be careful what he wished for.

Just then Ligniere burst into the empty theatre, pale and breathless, with his hat gone and his wine-flushed face drained of colour. He gasped out that he had written a song which mocked a great lord, and that a hundred hired men were now waiting at the Porte de Nesle, the very gate he must pass to reach his lodging. He had nowhere to sleep and nowhere to hide, and he begged his friends for protection.

Cyrano only laughed, and declared that he would walk the poet home himself and meet these hundred gentlemen on the way. Le Bret protested that it was madness and that no man alive could stand against such odds, but Cyrano answered that he was far too happy that night to be afraid of anything. Besides, he said, it would be a pity to waste such a splendid mood.

The news spread through the streets like fire, and soon the actors, the musicians, the soldiers and half the citizens of the neighbourhood had gathered, eager for a spectacle. Cyrano invited them all to follow him with torches and lanterns, on the condition that they would only watch and never interfere. A good fight, he said, was like a good poem, and ought to have an audience.

The strange procession wound through the sleeping streets of Paris, torches flaring, fiddles playing and Cyrano marching proudly at the front with Ligniere stumbling at his side. Overhead the moon rose over the rooftops and touched the old stones with silver. At last the little army halted in the shadows within sight of the Porte de Nesle, where the dark archway seemed to be waiting for them.

At the Porte de Nesle, Cyrano stepped alone into the narrow street and faced the hundred swordsmen who had come to harm his friend. His blade flickered like lightning, and those who did not fall back in alarm fell wounded, so that by the end of that wild night the way was free and Ligniere was safe. All Paris would talk of it for weeks, and Cyrano, who loved a great deed more than any prize, went home with his heart still singing.

Dawn was only just breaking over the roofs, but in the shop of Ragueneau the ovens were already roaring and the spits turning with a savoury hiss. Ragueneau himself, in a high white cap and a spotless apron, hurried from one tray to the next, humming a tune of his own invention. He was a cook by trade, but in his heart he was a poet, and the shop was the only one in Paris that smelled of both butter and rhyme.

The apprentices wrapped the warm tarts and little cakes in sheets of paper, and on every sheet there was a poem. They were the work of the poets who ate in the shop and paid for their breakfasts in verse, and Ragueneau, who loved every line, had no heart to refuse them. His wife Lise grumbled that she could not buy a single sack of flour with a sonnet, but the poets kept coming all the same.

Ragueneau climbed on a stool, struck a noble pose and proclaimed a recipe for almond tarts in the form of a long and flowing poem. His helpers laughed behind their floury hands, yet they listened carefully, for the rhymes were also very good instructions. The tarts that came out of the oven were golden and light, and it was a fair question whether the cook's art or the poet's deserved the credit.

Cyrano strolled through the door with his hat askew and his coat torn, looking tired but remarkably cheerful for a man who had not slept. Ragueneau dropped his ladle and hurried to greet him as though he were a king, for the whole city was already talking about the battle at the Porte de Nesle. Cyrano waved the praise aside and asked only for a chair, a pen and a quiet corner.

Cyrano explained that a lady was coming to the shop at the first hour, and that he needed it to be quiet and empty of poets for as long as she stayed. Ragueneau, who understood perfectly, winked and promised to keep every visitor away, even if it meant bolting the door and standing guard with a rolling pin. The hungry poets would have to eat their breakfasts in the street that morning, and they would not be pleased about it.

Alone at a table in the corner, Cyrano seized a pen and wrote the love letter that he had been carrying around in his head for months. When it was finished, he read it over twice, with his heart beating like a drum, and wondered whether he would ever find enough courage to put it into the lady's hands. He folded it carefully and slipped it inside his coat, close to his heart.

The Duenna arrived first, puffing from the walk, to announce that her mistress was just behind her. Cyrano, who wanted nothing more than to be alone with his cousin, piled a tray high with the shop's best cakes and ushered the old woman into the next room. She sat down with a sigh of pleasure, and within a minute the sound of busy chewing came through the door.

Roxane came into the shop like a ray of sunshine, her cheeks pink from the morning air and her eyes full of laughter. She crossed the room, took both of Cyrano's hands in hers, and called him her dear cousin in a voice that made the whole ugly world disappear. Cyrano, who could fence with a hundred men, found himself without a single word and could only bow.

Roxane laughed and reminded him of the summers of their childhood at Bergerac, when he had been her brave knight and her champion in all things. He had climbed the tallest trees for her and fought the village boys with a wooden sword, she said, and he had never once complained. Cyrano smiled, and in the smile there was a world of tenderness that she did not see.

Roxane thanked him warmly for the duel of the night before, saying that the Vicomte was precisely the man the Comte de Guiche wished her to marry. She had no more wish to wed that stuffed and perfumed puppet than to marry the moon, and she had laughed until she cried to see him pinned by the poet's point. Cyrano, hearing her laugh so freely at his side, felt a happiness so sharp that it almost hurt.

Roxane lowered her voice and told him that she had a secret which she could trust to nobody else, since he had been her friend and her brother-in-arms since they were children. Cyrano's heart gave a great leap against his ribs, and for one wild, bright moment he allowed himself to hope that the secret might be about him. His hands, held fast in hers, began to tremble like those of an old man in the cold.

Roxane blushed like a girl and confessed, with her eyes lowered and her fingers twisting her ribbon, that she was in love. Cyrano felt the colour drain from his face, for he did not yet know whether the hope in his heart was about to blossom or to perish. The silence in the shop seemed to stretch out for an hour before she spoke again.

Roxane explained, with shining eyes, that the man was a young soldier in the Cadets of Gascony, Cyrano's own company, so noble in his bearing that he must surely be as fine in his mind as in his face. They had never spoken, she admitted, and they had only exchanged glances in the theatre and in the street. Yet she was certain, with all the confidence of the young, that she had found her heart's choice.

Cyrano asked in a light, dry voice whether the young man was brave, whether he was clever, and whether he had ever said anything to prove it. He made a joke of every question to hide the pain that was tearing at him, and Roxane, who noticed nothing, replied that a man with such a face simply could not be anything but noble. The world, she said, would never have made such a face without a soul to match, and nobody could convince her otherwise.

Roxane confessed that she was frightened, for she knew how fierce the Gascons were, and how they loved to test every new recruit with a quarrel and a drawn sword. She begged her cousin to protect the young man, and above all to see that he never fought a duel on her account. Cyrano heard the request with a face of stone and said that it would be done.

Cyrano swore that the young man would come to no harm while he lived, and Roxane was so grateful that she clapped her hands like a child. She added one more favour, which was that Cyrano should ask the Cadet to write her a letter, since she longed to read his thoughts. Cyrano agreed to that too, and it seemed to him that every word he spoke was a nail driven into his own heart.

Roxane pressed his hands once more, thanked him in a rush of happy words, and hurried to the door. The Duenna trotted out of the next room behind her with her arms full of cakes and her mouth still full of crumbs, looking as pleased as any woman could after such a breakfast. Then the door swung shut, and Cyrano was left alone in the warm, sweet-smelling shop.

Alone at last, Cyrano sank into a chair and laughed a short, bitter laugh at the joke that fate had played on him. He had been asked to guard the very man who had won the heart that he wanted for himself, and he had given his word without a moment's hesitation. The folded letter inside his coat, so carefully written, now seemed as useless as a dead leaf.

The door crashed open, and the Cadets of Gascony tumbled in, led by their red-faced captain, Carbon de Castel-Jaloux, in a storm of boots, spurs and laughter. They had heard about the battle at the Porte de Nesle, and they had come at the run to cheer their most famous comrade. Their cloaks were patched and their purses were empty, but their moustaches bristled with pride.

The Cadets were a ragged company, poor as church mice and hungry as wolves, yet they carried their threadbare coats as proudly as if they had been cloth of gold. They hailed Cyrano as their champion, thumped him on the back, and called for food, wine and songs in a dozen different accents of the south. Ragueneau, who adored soldiers almost as much as poets, hurried to fetch his best tarts.

The Cadets begged him to tell the whole story of the fight at the Porte de Nesle, and Cyrano, who could have talked all day on any other subject, gave a short and modest answer. He said that it had been a pleasant walk, a little crowded, and that he had been glad of the exercise. The soldiers roared and drummed on the tables, for they knew a hero when they saw one.

The door opened, and the Comte de Guiche stepped into the shop with his chin high and his cloak trailing, and the cheerful uproar died as though a lid had been laid on it. The Cadets did not like him, for he was a favourite of the court, and they showed it by studying their boots and the ceiling. Cyrano alone looked at him directly, with his hat firmly on his head and an expression of perfect, polite indifference.

The Comte spoke with a smile like cold glass, saying that he had heard of Cyrano's tragedy Agrippine and admired it greatly. He offered to present it to the Cardinal Richelieu himself, who was known to love the theatre and who could make a poet rich and famous with a single word. It was, he implied, an extraordinary favour, and one that no sensible man would dream of refusing.

Then the Comte added, in the most careless tone in the world, that the Cardinal would naturally want a few lines changed here and there, as he always did with plays. It was a small thing, he said, a mere trifle, and a poet of sense would not mind it. Cyrano grew very still, and every Cadet in the shop leaned a little closer to hear the answer.

Cyrano thanked the Comte with great politeness and said that it was quite impossible, for he never changed so much as a comma of anything he wrote. The Cardinal might be the greatest man in France, but a poem was a poem, and he would rather see it burnt than improved by a stranger. The Cadets began to grin, and Le Bret covered his face with his hands.

Le Bret groaned aloud and said that his friend had thrown a fortune out of the window with both hands, while the Cadets cheered themselves hoarse at the refusal. Cyrano answered calmly that he would rather be a nobody who sang his own song than a great man who sang another's, and that he knew just what he was doing. For him, the price of such pride was a small one, and he would have paid it twice over without a moment's regret.

The Comte, white with anger, remarked that Cyrano's pride would be the ruin of him one day, and he swept out of the shop with a swirl of his cloak. Cyrano called after him a joke so neat and so wounding that the Cadets collapsed on the benches, weeping with laughter. Even Ragueneau, who had never thrown a witty word in his life, applauded as though he were in the theatre.

Captain Carbon called the company to order and brought forward a handsome young man who had only just joined it, Christian de Neuvillette. The Cadets, who never missed a chance for mischief, whispered in his ear that whatever else he did, he must on no account mention Cyrano's nose. They enjoyed this trick enormously, and they waited with shining eyes to see what would happen.

Christian, who was determined not to be thought a coward, did exactly what the Cadets had hoped, and made a clumsy joke about Cyrano's nose in a loud and nervous voice. The shop went dead silent, and every Cadet held his breath, expecting to see the newcomer cut in half on the spot. The silence was so thick and so heavy that nobody dared to move a finger or even to cough.

Cyrano turned white and gripped the back of a chair until his knuckles cracked, and for a moment the Cadets thought that blood would flow. But he remembered whose face he was looking at, and whose name he had sworn to protect, and by a tremendous effort he forced his rage down. When he spoke at last, his voice was soft and quite steady, and it held no trace of the storm inside him.

Cyrano called the young man over, shook his hand with surprising warmth, and led him to a quiet corner of the shop away from the astonished Cadets. There, in a low voice, he told Christian that he was the cousin of Roxane, the very lady who had been filling the young man's thoughts. Christian, who had expected a sword and had received a handshake instead, could only stare at him in bewilderment.

Cyrano told him that the lady had noticed him from afar and had lost her heart to him, and that she had sent word through her cousin to ask him to write. Christian could scarcely believe his ears and made Cyrano repeat every word twice, his face glowing with disbelief and delight. He wanted to apologise for his rudeness, to laugh aloud, and to dance around the shop all at the same moment.

Then, quite suddenly, Christian's face fell, for the thought of actually speaking to Roxane had come to him. He confessed that he was a poor talker and a worse writer, and that so clever a lady would soon grow tired of a man whose only gift was his face. He had been brave a thousand times in the field, he said, but he had never yet been brave with words.

Cyrano considered the matter for a moment, and then he spoke with sudden sparkling energy. He would lend the young man his wit, and the young man would lend him his handsome face and his figure, and between them they would make a single hero of whom any woman might dream. It was, he said, the perfect bargain, since each of them possessed exactly what the other lacked.

Christian accepted at once with a stammer of wonder, and Cyrano drew from his coat the letter that he had written that very morning, carefully folded and full of burning words. He told the young man to copy it out, to learn it by heart, and to send it to Roxane as though it were his own. If Christian suspected what it cost him to give it away, he said nothing.

In the days that followed, Cyrano wrote letter after letter in Christian's name, sitting late into the night by a single guttering candle while the city slept. He wrote of the stars, of the sea, of the ache of absence and the sweetness of hope, and he never complained of weariness. Each morning Christian copied out the pages in his own handwriting and carried them away, a happy messenger who never guessed what he carried.

In her small, lamplit room, Roxane read each letter three times over and kissed the page before she put it away. She told her old servant, with tears of pleasure in her eyes, that no poet in all Paris could write so tenderly as her Christian, and that she loved him more with every line. The pile of letters beside her bed grew taller every day, tied up with a ribbon like a precious treasure.

One night, as he wrote, a single tear fell on the paper and smudged a line, and Cyrano saw with a shock how much of himself he had poured into those pages. They were Christian's letters in name only, and every sentence was a confession of the love that he could never speak under his own. He smiled sadly and wrote on, for it was the only way he would ever tell her.

Meanwhile, poor Ragueneau had come to the end of his fortune, for the poets had eaten his stock to the last crumb and his wife Lise had run away with a handsome musketeer. He stood in the empty shop with tears pouring down his floury cheeks, searching for a rope to end his troubles. It was Cyrano, arriving at the very last minute, who snatched it out of his hands.

Cyrano scolded the weeping cook for his foolishness, reminded him that a poet had more to live for than any baker, and promised to find him a better post before the week was out. A few days later he had arranged for Ragueneau to enter Roxane's house as a servant, where there was a kitchen that needed him and a mistress who loved verses. The cook dried his eyes, and for the first time that week he smiled.

Several weeks had passed since the first of the letters, and evening was falling softly over the quiet street where Roxane lived. Her house had a little garden behind a stone wall, and a balcony hung with jasmine looked down over the dusk, filling the air with sweetness. It was exactly the sort of place in which a young woman might lie awake dreaming of a poet.

In the kitchen, Ragueneau, now in the service of Roxane, sat scribbling poems on the back of the shopping list while a pot boiled over unnoticed. The Duenna scolded him loudly for forgetting the bread, the butter and the candles, but the poet only smiled and went on rhyming. He had lost his shop, his wife and his savings, yet he was happier than he had ever been, for he was surrounded by poetry.

Roxane told the Duenna, with a glow of excitement that she could not hide, that Christian was coming to see her that evening. She had read his beautiful letters for weeks, and had kept them under her pillow like treasure, and now she longed to hear the voice that had written them. She was quite sure that it would be even finer than the words, and she meant to tell him so.

Roxane took a letter from her sleeve and read part of it aloud, sighing with pleasure at every phrase. The Duenna, who had seen a great many lovers in her day, shrugged and remarked that in her long experience a man was usually either handsome or clever, and almost never both. Roxane only laughed and said that the Duenna had clearly never had the good fortune to meet Christian.

Suddenly a servant hurried in to announce that the Comte de Guiche was at the door, and Roxane's face fell with annoyance. She hid her letters beneath a cushion, whispered an order to the Duenna to say nothing at all about Christian, and arranged herself in a chair with an expression of calm courtesy. A moment later the Comte de Guiche strode into the room, filling the doorway with his plumes and his importance.

The Comte de Guiche entered in a gleaming soldier's breastplate, with a plumed hat in his hand and a gravity that did not suit him. He told Roxane that his regiment was leaving that night for the siege of Arras, and that he could not go without seeing her once more. His voice was soft, and for a moment she almost felt sorry for him.

Then the Comte added, almost as an afterthought, that the Cadets of Gascony, Cyrano's own company, would march to Arras with the rest of the army. Roxane grew pale, for she knew very well that Christian was one of them and that he would be sent into the thick of the fighting. She gripped the arms of her chair until her fingers ached, but she kept her voice light and her smile in place.

Roxane thought quickly, and in a voice of sweet innocence she asked the Comte how he might best punish Cyrano for his insolence. Nothing would hurt a man like that, she suggested, so much as being left behind in Paris with his whole company, idle and ashamed, while the other regiments marched off to glory. Cyrano would be furious at such an insult, she said, and the Cadets would never forgive their leader for it.

The Comte laughed with delight, supposing that Roxane had at last taken his side against her cousin, and he swore to give the order at once. He kissed her hand with great feeling, and she let him do it, though every nerve in her body longed to pull away. Secretly she thanked heaven, for she believed that she had just kept her Christian out of the war.

At the door the Comte turned and promised that he would send a messenger to her house later that night with a letter, and that he hoped to see her once more before he marched. Roxane curtsied politely and waited until his footsteps had faded down the street, and then she picked up her skirts and ran to the garden. The stars were coming out, and somewhere in the darkness Christian was on his way.

Christian arrived in the dark street below the balcony with Cyrano at his side, and announced with surprising confidence that he had learned how to talk to a lady and would speak for himself that night. He had been practising, he explained, all through the evening, and he was tired of being the puppet of another man's wit. Cyrano, hiding a smile, only shrugged his shoulders and stepped back into the deep shadows to watch what would happen.

Roxane stepped out onto the balcony in a cloud of jasmine and asked him in her soft voice to tell her about his love. Christian opened his mouth, and all that he could say, again and again and again, was that he loved her, that he loved her very much, and that he loved her more than anything. The brave soldier had been struck dumb, and every fine word had flown out of his head.

Roxane listened for a long time, and then she told him gently that this was nothing like the letters, and that she had hoped for words more worthy of a poet. She said that a plain declaration of love was not enough for her, and she turned and went back into the house, closing the shutters behind her. Christian was left alone in the dark street, his face hot with shame and his hands hanging helplessly at his sides.

Christian, nearly in tears, called desperately for Cyrano to help him, and the swordsman stepped out of the darkness with a patient smile. He said that he had expected nothing else, for no man could be expected to learn the art of speaking to ladies in a single afternoon. Then he told his friend to knock at the door again, and to leave the rest to him.

Cyrano slipped into the blackest part of the shadow beneath the balcony, where nobody could see him, and Christian called softly up to Roxane's window. After a moment the shutters opened again and she came out, a little curious and a little cold, to see whether he had anything more to say. Christian, who now had a helper, only took a deep breath and began to repeat what was whispered to him.

Cyrano whispered the lines one after another from the shadow, and Christian repeated them aloud, but so slowly and so stiffly that the beauty of the words was nearly lost. Roxane, who was no fool, laughed down at him and asked why he spoke so very slowly that evening, and why his words seemed to come from somewhere else. Cyrano groaned silently and decided that it was time to take matters into his own hands.

Cyrano could bear it no longer, and he pushed Christian aside and spoke up to the balcony himself, in a low and tender voice that the night seemed to carry like music. Roxane leaned eagerly over the railing and listened, for it was exactly the voice she had imagined behind the letters. If she noticed that it had changed a little, she thought only that the darkness had given him courage.

He spoke of the stars above them, of the scent of jasmine and of the strange freedom of speaking in the dark, when a man need not fear a lady's eyes. The words poured out of him like water from a spring that had been blocked for years, and Roxane listened with her hands pressed to her breast. She said, in a trembling voice, that she had never heard anything so beautiful in her life.

Roxane confessed that she longed for a kiss, and Cyrano, trembling from head to foot, answered her with a speech about what a kiss truly is. He said that it was a promise made at the closest possible range, a secret told to the lips rather than to the ear, and a sweet seal set upon a heart that has already given itself away. Every word of it was his own, and every word of it was meant for her.

Cyrano seized Christian by the sleeve, pushed him toward the wall, and told him to climb up and claim the kiss that had been so nobly earned. Christian scrambled up the jasmine and over the rail, and the two shadows on the balcony melted together while Cyrano stood below with his hat in his hand. He felt that he had given a gift, and that a small, bitter part of it had been given back to him.

While the lovers were still whispering, the Duenna came bustling into the garden to announce that a monk was at the front door asking for her mistress. He was a Capuchin, she said, an old and short-sighted man in a brown robe, and he carried a letter from a great nobleman. Roxane drew back from the railing with a start, for she could guess very well whose letter it was.

The old Capuchin had been peering at the doors along the street for half an hour, for his eyes were weak and the house numbers were hard to read in the dark. He bowed politely when he found the right lady, and handed Roxane the letter from the Comte de Guiche, which she tore open with a frown. By the light of a lantern she read that the Comte had not marched, and that he would come to her that very night.

Roxane held the letter up to the lantern and read it aloud with great solemnity, but at the crucial point she began to invent. According to her version, the Comte begged the holy father to marry her to Christian de Neuvillette that very night, in secret, as a sacrifice that his noble heart had decided to make. It was a bold, shameless lie, and it was delivered with the sweetest face in Paris.

The honest old monk, who had never in his life suspected anybody of deceit, was deeply touched by the generosity of the Comte. He declared that the great man's soul was nobler than he had supposed, and that it would be an honour to perform the marriage without any delay at all. Roxane thanked him with tears in her eyes, and the tears, at least, were perfectly real.

Roxane led the monk into the house, followed by the Duenna and a dazed and delighted Christian, and told Cyrano in a whisper to keep watch outside. If the Comte should appear, she said, he must be kept away from the door at any price. Cyrano nodded, and the door closed behind them with a soft click, leaving him alone in the dark street.

Alone in the dark street, Cyrano leaned against the wall and thought of the little ceremony going on inside the house, with its candles and its whispered vows. The woman he loved was being married to the man who had borrowed his words, and all that remained to him was to guard the door. He smiled, a little crookedly, and decided that a guard ought at least to do his duty well.

A cloaked figure with a mask over his eyes crept along the street toward Roxane's house, glancing over his shoulder at every step. Cyrano knew the Comte de Guiche in an instant, for nobody else in Paris walked with such a careful air of importance, and he saw that the man had come back in secret instead of marching to the war. Cyrano needed to delay him, and he needed to think of a way to do it before the man reached the door.

Cyrano scrambled up the garden wall, swung himself out on a branch and let himself drop with a tremendous thump directly in front of the astonished Comte. He lay perfectly still on the cobbles for a moment, as though he had fallen out of the sky itself, and then he sat up slowly and rubbed his head. The Comte, who had leaped back with a cry, drew his sword in alarm.

Cyrano rose slowly to his feet, looked around with a dazed air, and asked the Comte in the politest tone what country this might be, and what year, and what hour of the night. Then he declared with perfect gravity that he had just that moment fallen from the moon. The Comte, who had been expecting a murderer or a thief, was completely taken aback.

Cyrano proceeded to explain, in the most solemn and scientific manner, exactly how a man might travel to the moon, with bottles of morning dew tied to his belt, with rockets and mirrors, and with the pull of the tide. Each method was more ridiculous than the last, and each was told with such lively conviction that the Comte, in spite of himself, stood listening with his mouth half open. All the while the clock was ticking on, and inside the house the wedding was moving steadily toward its end.

At last the door of the house opened, and the old Capuchin came out into the lantern light with a gentle smile and a blessing on his lips. The wedding was done, and Cyrano, who had been watching the doorway out of the corner of his eye, ended his story of the moon in the middle of a sentence and swept off his hat with a flourish. The Comte stared at him, and a terrible suspicion began to dawn in his face.

Roxane and Christian stepped out of the doorway hand in hand, glowing like two lanterns, and Roxane told the Comte calmly that he had come too late to prevent the match. She and Christian de Neuvillette had just been married, she said, and she thanked him for sending such an excellent monk. The Comte went white to the lips, and his hand tightened slowly on the hilt of his sword.

The truth struck the Comte all at once: the false letter, the faithful monk, the story of the moon and the closed door had all been parts of a single trick. He looked from Roxane to Cyrano and back again, shaking with fury, while the good monk stood bewildered between them, understanding nothing. For a long moment there was no sound in the street but the harsh rasp of the Comte's breathing and the thin cry of a distant owl.

In his rage the Comte reversed the order he had given earlier that evening and declared that the Cadets of Gascony would not remain in Paris after all. They would march to the war at Arras that very night, and they would be sent to the hottest post in the lines. If the bridegroom wanted his bride, he said bitterly, he would have to win her back from the enemy.

Roxane threw herself on his mercy and begged him to spare her new husband, but the Comte answered coldly that the order was given and that it could not be changed. Cyrano, with a mocking bow, assured him that the Cadets of Gascony would be delighted to see a real battle at last. The Comte turned on his heel and strode away into the dark, his cloak flying behind him.

When the Comte had gone, Roxane turned to her cousin with tears shining in her eyes and made him swear that he would watch over her husband in the war. She begged him, too, to make sure that Christian wrote to her every single day, without ever missing one. Cyrano promised on his honour, thinking privately that the letters would be the easiest part of the bargain.

In the darkness of the garden, Roxane clung to her husband and whispered a farewell so tender that it might have broken a heart of stone. Cyrano, who stood a little way off, turned his back to them and studied the stars with great attention, trying not to hear a word. It was the first night of their marriage, and they were to be parted before the dawn.

Drums began to roll along the street, and the Cadets of Gascony came tumbling out of every doorway, buckling on their swords and shouldering their muskets. Captain Carbon stood at the head of the column and called the roll in a voice that rattled the shutters. They were still laughing and joking, for the Cadets thought of war as a kind of holiday.

At last the column marched off into the night, singing a song of the south at the top of its voice, while Roxane stood on her balcony and waved a white handkerchief until the last figure had vanished. Cyrano looked back once at the balcony where he had spoken the finest words of his life, and then he turned his face to the road. In his coat was a letter that he had promised to write, and he meant to write it.

On the long road north the army halted at nightfall, and the Cadets made camp in a field, stretching their tired legs around a dozen fires. By the light of one of them, Cyrano took out paper and a stub of pencil and began the first of the daily letters that he had promised to write. Christian slept nearby with a smile on his face, and the stars wheeled slowly overhead.

At the siege of Arras, a grey and sullen dawn rose over a camp of leaking tents and muddy ditches, with the high walls of the town looming through the mist. The French had surrounded the city, but the Spanish army had come up behind them and cut off the roads, so that the besiegers had become besieged themselves. Nobody could leave the camp without being seen, and almost nothing at all could get in from the outside.

The Cadets of Gascony had eaten almost nothing for days, and they lay wrapped in their thin cloaks around the dead fires, pale, hollow-cheeked and silent. The army's bread had run out and the supply wagons could not get through, so that the only meal anyone could be sure of was a handful of hard crumbs. Even so, not one of them was willing to admit how hungry he was.

An old Cadet took out a little pipe and began to play a tune from the hills of Gascony, a slow and wistful song that every man in the camp had heard in his cradle. One by one the soldiers lifted their heads, and the hard faces grew soft with longing for home, for green valleys, for mothers and for mountains far away. Some of the toughest fighters in France wiped their eyes on their ragged sleeves.

Cyrano strode into the middle of the camp and shouted that men who wept at a tune were not fit to be soldiers of Gascony, or soldiers of anywhere else. He reminded them of the Porte de Nesle and the hundred men, and of all the glorious times that they had laughed at danger, and he made such a comic speech of it that the tears turned into laughter. Within a minute the whole camp was in a roar of laughter, and the pipe had been quite forgotten.

Long before the sun was up, Cyrano pulled a dark cloak over his shoulders, tucked a freshly written letter inside his coat, and slipped silently out of the sleeping camp. The sentries did not see him go, and the Cadets lay snoring in the damp grass, unaware that their friend was leaving on the most dangerous errand of the war. He had done exactly the same thing every single morning since the army had first reached Arras.

Cyrano crept through the mist on his hands and knees, slipping between the Spanish sentries, lying flat in ditches and holding his breath whenever a foot crunched nearby. He knew the way by now almost as well as his own room, and he knew that one mistake would mean a bullet. He did not rest until the letter was safe in the hands of a messenger who would carry it to Paris.

Cyrano came back at nightfall with a bullet hole through his hat and a long scratch on his arm, whistling as cheerfully as a boy returning from school. Le Bret, who had spent the entire day sick with worry, scolded him angrily for risking his life for the sake of a mere letter. Cyrano only smiled, and said that he had given his word and that his word was worth more than his skin.

Christian, who had noticed the empty blanket every morning and the mud on Cyrano's boots every night, finally asked what his friend did each day beyond the lines. Cyrano answered lightly that he went to post the letter, and that a morning walk through the mist was a pleasant way to keep fit. Christian stared at him, understanding for the first time how much that walk really cost.

That night, Christian asked what Cyrano had written to Roxane that day, and Cyrano recited a few lines from memory in the firelight. They were so tender and so splendid that the Cadets stopped their grumbling and gathered round, and for a moment even the hungry were not thinking of bread. Christian listened with a face that was half pride and half sadness, and he said nothing at all until the lines were done.

At dawn the next morning, a sentry cried out in a cracked voice that a coach was rolling across the fields toward the camp, and the Cadets scrambled to their feet in blank amazement. Some of them rubbed their eyes, sure that hunger had given them visions, while others reached for their muskets in case it was a Spanish trick. But it was real: a grand coach, with six horses, was bouncing over the ruts.

Behind the coach, the Spanish soldiers stood in a row along their trench with their guns lowered, and some of them were even touching their hats. Nobody had fired a single shot at the grand vehicle, which had trundled through the enemy lines as calmly as if it were rolling down a country lane. The Cadets stared at the Spaniards across the field, and the Spaniards stared back at them, equally puzzled and equally amused.

The coach lurched into the camp with Ragueneau sitting up on the driver's box in magnificent livery, his cap on one ear and his face one great grin. He pulled up the steaming horses, the door swung open, and Roxane stepped down into the mud as lightly as if it had been a ballroom floor. The ragged Cadets stood with their mouths open, as though an angel had descended in the middle of the camp.

Roxane laughed and explained that she had crossed the enemy lines by telling the truth. At every post, she had told the Spanish officers that she was going to see the man she loved, and each of those gallant gentlemen had smiled, bowed low and waved the coach through. Love, she said, was a passport that every country respected, and no soldier in Europe could refuse it.

Ragueneau, with the air of a magician revealing his finest trick, threw open the boot of the coach and displayed a treasure of hams, pies, roast chickens, loaves and bottles of wine. The starving Cadets gave a roar that shook the tents, and one poor fellow was so overcome that he had to sit down on the ground. Ragueneau, who had spent his life feeding poets, had never been so well appreciated.

The Cadets feasted, a little shy in the presence of a lady and extremely polite, and Roxane went from man to man serving them with her own hands. The roughest fighters in the army bowed their heads, begged her pardon for their torn coats and thanked her in voices that had suddenly become gentle. Within an hour the camp, which had been silent and grey, was full of laughter and the smell of roast meat.

In the middle of the feast the Comte de Guiche rode into the camp, and the soldiers fell quiet and stiffened, their mouths still full of ham. He was astonished to see Roxane standing among them with a bottle in her hand, but he bowed to her with all the old courtesy of the court. She inclined her head to him in return, coolly, and went on pouring wine.

The Comte lowered his voice and warned the officers that scouts had brought word of a great Spanish attack, which would fall upon the camp at dawn. He advised Roxane to take her coach and leave at once while it was still possible, but she told him quietly that she would not go, since her husband was here. The Comte looked at her for a moment, and something in his face changed.

To everyone's surprise, the Comte announced that he too would stay and fight at the side of the Cadets, since a nobleman who ran from danger would be a poor commander. A whisper of amazement ran through the ranks, and Cyrano, who had always despised the man, was obliged to admit that the decision took real courage. Perhaps, he thought, there was more to the Comte than a pair of fine boots.

Roxane asked where her husband was, and the Cadets looked at one another and began to search the camp. Cyrano found Christian sitting alone behind the tents, pale and silent, and brought him gently back to his wife. When Roxane saw him she ran forward with a cry and threw her arms around his neck, and the Cadets discreetly turned away.

While the Cadets ate politely at a distance, Roxane drew her husband down beside her on a fallen log and held his hands in hers. She told him, with her face glowing, that his letters had made her love him a hundred times more than she had ever done on the night of their wedding. Christian listened, and a small, cold doubt began to stir somewhere deep in his heart, like a stone dropped in a well.

Roxane told him softly that in the beginning she had loved him for his beauty, as any girl might love a handsome face in a theatre. But the letters had taught her something deeper, she said, and now it was his soul that she loved, as it shone out of every one of his lines. She had never known such happiness in all her life, she said, and she wished that it could last for ever.

Christian asked her, in a strange, tight voice, whether she would love him just the same if he were plain, or even ugly. Roxane answered without a moment's hesitation that she would, for it was the soul and not the face that she had fallen in love with. She meant it with all her heart, and she did not know that every word of it struck him like a blow.

Christian went white to the lips, for he had understood at last what her words really meant. The soul that she loved was the soul of the letters, and the soul of the letters belonged not to him but to his friend, who had written every line. He had married a woman who loved the wrong man, and the wrong man was himself.

Roxane drew a worn letter from the folds of her dress and read a passage from it aloud, sighing happily between the lines. Each tender word, so beautiful in itself and so cruel in the ears of the man who had borrowed it, made Christian suffer a little more than the one before. He sat with his eyes on the ground and his hands clasped tightly together.

Roxane kissed her husband tenderly and went off to rest in the coach with the Duenna, tired by her long and hazardous journey. Christian stood watching her walk away across the trampled grass, with her skirts rustling and her head held high, and a heavy sadness settled on his shoulders like a cloak of lead. He knew with a terrible clearness that she had never really been talking to him at all, but to a ghost.

Christian went to Cyrano and told him, in a low and bitter voice, that it was Cyrano whom Roxane really loved, and not himself. Cyrano denied it at once, hastily, and said that it was a mistake born of the heat, the hunger and the excitement of the journey. But the denial was too quick and too loud, and Christian only shook his head.

Christian insisted that Cyrano must tell Roxane the whole truth, from the first letter to the last word under the balcony. She had a right to know who had written to her and who had spoken in the dark, he said, and then she must be free to choose whichever of them she wanted. He would abide by her choice, he promised, whatever it was, and whichever of them she wished to keep.

Cyrano refused at first, afraid that the truth would lose Roxane for them both, and that it would break the heart of a woman who had done nothing wrong. But Christian was so earnest and so unhappy that in the end Cyrano saw he was right, and slowly, with a heavy heart, he agreed to tell her. Perhaps, he thought, this was the one chance he would ever be given to hear her say what she truly felt.

Christian walked off between the tents to fetch Roxane, and Cyrano was left alone beside the cold ashes of the fire, staring at his own hands. He was afraid of what he must say, and he was even more afraid of what she might answer when she had heard it. For years he had longed for this moment, and now that it had come, he almost wished it away.

Suddenly a cannon boomed in the distance, and then another, and then a whole line of them, while a drum began to roll along the camp. The Cadets seized their muskets and swords and ran to their places, and Cyrano, with his own business abandoned, ran with them. The great Spanish attack that the Comte de Guiche had warned them of had come at last, exactly as he had said it would.

The Spanish army came across the field in a great wave, shouting, with banners flying and the early light flashing on their weapons. The Comte de Guiche rode along the line, and in a clear voice he ordered the Cadets to hold their post at any cost until help could come. The Cadets, hungry and ragged and fierce, answered him with a roar and levelled their guns.

Ragueneau and the Duenna bundled Roxane into the coach, and though she cried out that she wished to stay with her husband, Cyrano told her gently but firmly that she must go. The horses were whipped into a gallop, and the grand vehicle bounced away across the fields toward a safer part of the camp. Roxane looked back through the little window of the coach until she could no longer see Christian among the smoke and the soldiers.

Christian, who was braver than any man of letters, charged out in front of the line to protect a wounded comrade from the enemy. A bullet struck him squarely in the chest, and he fell to the ground with a look of surprise on his handsome face. The battle roared on around him, and for a few terrible seconds nobody noticed.

Cyrano saw the young man fall and ran across the open field to him, ignoring the bullets that hummed past his ears like angry wasps. He dropped to his knees beside Christian and lifted his head very gently onto his arm, and the great swordsman's hands were trembling. Christian opened his eyes and looked up at the sky, and then at the face above him.

Christian asked in a faint whisper whether Cyrano had told Roxane the truth, and whom she had chosen. Cyrano, who had not been given the time, looked into his dying friend's eyes and told him a kind and gentle lie, that she loved him, and him alone. It was the last gift that he could offer, and he gave it with all his heart.

Christian smiled, as though he had been given something precious, and his head fell back against Cyrano's arm. Over his heart, tucked inside his coat, was a last letter that Cyrano had written in his name days before, in case such a moment should come, and now Cyrano's own tears were falling upon it. The young soldier was gone, and the only man who had known him truly was weeping over his body.

Cyrano rose slowly to his feet with tears still wet on his cheeks, and then he snatched up his sword and let out a cry that rose above the thunder of the guns. He called the Cadets to him, and they followed him in a furious charge that smashed into the enemy ranks like a hammer against glass. It seemed as though he fought for two men that morning, and perhaps in his heart he truly did.

At last the Spanish ranks broke, and the enemy retreated across the field, and the thunder of the guns faded slowly into silence. Many brave Cadets lay on the trampled grass, and the survivors stood leaning on their muskets, too tired to cheer. The Comte de Guiche, who had fought like a lion beside them, took off his hat to the Cadets and bowed his head.

Roxane came running back across the silent field, her skirts torn and her face white, and found her husband lying where he had fallen. She knelt beside him in the grass, kissed his cold forehead, and drew from his coat the letter that lay over his heart, stained with blood and with tears. Cyrano stood a little way off with his head bowed, unable to say a single word.

Roxane read the last letter slowly through her tears, and every tender word seemed to pierce her heart as she followed it down the page. Cyrano, who knew each one by heart because he had written them himself, stood in silence a few steps away and heard his own love spoken aloud for another man's funeral. The wet marks on the paper were partly Christian's blood and partly his own tears.

When the war was over, Roxane put on black, left the world behind her and retired to a quiet convent outside Paris to mourn for the husband she had lost. Cyrano walked with her as far as the gate, and although the truth rose to his lips a dozen times on the way, he said nothing of it. He promised only that he would visit her there as often as the sisters would allow.

Fifteen years passed, and in the autumn of 1655 the garden of the convent was as still and golden as a painting, with its gravel paths and its old stone bench. Leaves fell slowly from the great tree in the middle of the lawn, and the sisters moved softly along the paths like shadows in grey robes. Nothing seemed to have changed since the day Roxane first came there, and yet everything had.

Sister Marthe and Sister Claire walked together under the great tree, whispering about the lady in black who had lived among them for fifteen years. She was as faithful in her grief as any saint, they agreed, and as gentle as a dove, yet there was only one visitor in the whole world who could ever make her laugh. The two sisters looked at each other and smiled, for they both knew perfectly well who that visitor was and when he would come.

Roxane sat at her embroidery frame beneath the tree, dressed in black from head to foot, with her needle moving slowly through the cloth. On a ribbon around her neck hung a little silk bag, and inside it lay Christian's last letter, folded small, with the old stains still on it. She had read it so many times that she knew it better than any prayer.

Every Saturday for fifteen years, as the clock struck the hour, Cyrano had come through the garden gate to sit beside Roxane and tell her the news of Paris. He called it his Gazette, and it was so full of wit and mischief that the old stone walls seemed to echo with laughter whenever he spoke. In all that time he had never missed a single week, and he had never been late.

In those fifteen years Cyrano had stayed as poor and as proud as ever, refusing every patron and every pension that anyone offered him. He wrote what he pleased and said what he thought, and he had made a great many new enemies by laughing at the false, the greedy and the cowardly wherever he found them. Yet he had never changed, and he walked through Paris with his head high and his hat cocked.

Le Bret and Ragueneau came into the garden that afternoon with troubled faces and spoke to Roxane in low voices. They told her that Cyrano was far poorer than he would ever admit, that he lived alone in a bare room without a fire, and that he had dangerous enemies waiting for him in every corner of Paris. Roxane listened with growing alarm, and her embroidery slipped unnoticed from her fingers onto the grass.

Roxane smiled gently at their worry and told them that they need not be afraid on his account, since Cyrano had been in danger all his life and had always come out of it laughing. She said that he was the bravest and the most cheerful man she had ever known, and that no one could harm him. She spoke with such confidence that Le Bret did not have the heart to contradict her.

The Comte de Guiche, who had since become a duke and a great man of the realm, rolled up to the convent in a splendid coach and came to speak to Roxane under the tree. He had every honour that a man could want, he said, and yet he found himself envying the one man in France who had never bowed to anyone. He warned her that Cyrano's enemies were growing bolder, and he meant it kindly.

The Duke bowed and left, and the convent bells began to strike the hour while the leaves drifted down around the old stone bench. Roxane counted the strokes under her breath, as she did each week, for Cyrano always came through the gate on the very last of them. This time, however, the last stroke died away, and the gate stayed closed, and the garden was silent.

Earlier that afternoon, as Cyrano walked through a quiet street toward the convent, a heavy log of wood dropped from a high window and struck him squarely on the head. It had been let fall deliberately by a hired servant of one of his many enemies, who preferred an ambush to a duel and did not care to be seen. Cyrano fell to the cobbles without a sound, and for a long moment the quiet street seemed to hold its breath.

After a long time Cyrano struggled to his feet, dizzy and bleeding from a terrible blow, and with unsteady fingers he pulled his hat down low over the wound. He knew perfectly well that it was serious, and he knew that a sensible man would call a doctor and lie down. But it was Saturday, and nothing on earth was going to keep him from the convent garden.

Cyrano climbed the long road toward the convent step by painful step, leaning on garden walls, resting on doorsteps and using his sword as a walking stick. The blood crept down inside his collar, and the world swam before his eyes, but each time his strength failed he thought of the woman waiting in the garden and went on. He would be late, he knew, for the first time in all those years, but he would certainly come.

At last the gate creaked open, and Cyrano walked slowly into the garden, very pale, with his hat pulled low over his brows. Roxane looked up with a smile and teased him gently that for the first time in fifteen years, the most punctual man in Paris had kept her waiting. Cyrano bowed, as gracefully as he could manage, and said that he had been detained by a tiresome visitor.

Cyrano lowered himself carefully onto the stone bench beside Roxane, and with something very like his old sparkle he began to deliver the week's Gazette. He told her of weddings and quarrels, of the fashions at court and the follies of the great, and he made each story so absurd that she was laughing within a minute. If his voice grew a little fainter as he went on, she was too happy to notice.

Roxane stopped laughing at last and looked at him more closely, and she saw that his face was as white as paper and that his voice was growing faint. She asked in alarm what was the matter, and Cyrano shrugged and said that it was nothing, only the old wound from Arras troubling him again. It was a good lie, and he told it so lightly that she almost believed him.

Roxane said, quietly, that everyone had an old wound of one kind or another, and that hers was here, and she touched the little silk bag that hung at her throat. Inside it lay the last letter that Christian had written, stained with his blood and with the tears that had fallen on it, and she wore it still. Cyrano watched her slender fingers close around it, and his heart ached with a tenderness that he had never been able to put into words.

Cyrano asked, in a very gentle voice, whether he might be allowed to read the letter that she kept over her heart. Roxane was surprised, for in fifteen years he had never once asked to see it, but after a moment's hesitation she took it from its bag and laid it in his hands. The paper was soft with age and brown at the edges, and it was marked here and there with dark stains that had never faded.

Cyrano unfolded the old letter with great care, held it up to the failing light and began to read aloud in a low, steady voice. The sun was sinking behind the trees, and the gold of the garden was turning grey, and the shadows of the leaves lengthened across the grass. Roxane leaned back against the bench and listened, with her hands folded in her lap.

The words of the farewell letter flowed out of him: the writer told Roxane that he was about to die, that his whole heart was full of her, and that he would go on loving her beyond the grave. He said that he had never known anyone so dear and that he asked for nothing, except that she should sometimes remember him. Roxane listened with tears running down her cheeks, as she had listened a hundred times before.

Dusk gathered thickly in the garden, the first lights glimmered in the convent windows, and the shadows beneath the great tree turned from grey to black. Cyrano went on reading the letter in the same low, steady voice, without any hesitation, though the page in his hands had long since faded into the dark. Roxane, soothed by the sound and lost in her own memories, did not at first notice that anything was strange.

All at once Roxane noticed that the dusk had grown so deep that no one could possibly read a word on the page. Yet Cyrano's voice had not paused or stumbled, and he was no longer looking at the paper but staring straight ahead into the darkness. She sat up very slowly, and her heart began to beat faster as a wild and wonderful suspicion crept into her mind.

Roxane rose slowly from the bench and stared at him in the dusk, and another night came back to her, a night of jasmine and starlight and a voice speaking out of the dark beneath her balcony. It was the same voice, soft and warm and full of passion, that had spoken to her out of the darkness so long ago, and it seemed to be speaking again now. She had heard it every single Saturday for fifteen years, and she had never once known it for what it was.

Roxane cried out in a voice full of wonder and grief that it had been he, from the very beginning, and that she ought to have known. He had been the voice at the balcony and the hand that wrote every letter, and the soul that she had loved for fifteen years was his and no one else's. The words burst out of her all together, like water from a broken dam, and she could not have stopped them if she had tried.

Cyrano denied it at first, with a feeble laugh, and said that she was dreaming, that it was Christian whom she had loved, and that he himself had merely been a friend. But his voice shook, his hands trembled, and every word he said only made the truth plainer, until at last he fell silent and bowed his head. He had no strength left to lie, and perhaps, in his heart, he had no wish to go on lying any longer.

Roxane said, weeping, that she ought to have known long ago, and that all those years she had held the proof against her heart. The tears upon the letter had not been Christian's, she said, but had been shed by the one man who had loved her enough to write the words and then to give them away. She had been blind for fifteen years, and he had let her be blind rather than break her heart.

Cyrano answered softly that Christian had been young and handsome and brave, and that he himself had been nothing but the voice and the pen, a shadow behind a lovelier man. He had never wanted her pity, he said, and he was glad that she had loved something, even if it was only a dream made of his words. That, he told her gently, had been enough for him, and he had never wished for anything more than that.

Roxane held his hand in both of hers and wept that she had loved only one soul in her whole life, and that she had lost it twice. She had lost it once on the battlefield at Arras when she thought it was Christian's, and now she was losing it again in the dusk of the garden, when she knew it was his. The first stars appeared above the convent wall, small and cold and very far away, as the garden sank into darkness.

At that moment Le Bret and Ragueneau came running into the garden, breathless and frightened, calling out Cyrano's name. They had just learned that an enemy had dropped a log upon his head from a window, and that the wounded man had somehow dragged himself all the way up the hill to the convent. They reproached him bitterly for not calling a doctor, and their voices shook with love and with fear for the man they had known so long.

Roxane reached out and lifted his hat gently, and when she saw the blood-soaked bandage beneath it, she understood everything at once. He had been dying through the whole of that afternoon, and he had come all the way to the convent to tell her the news of Paris, with a smile on his lips. Her grief and her love together were more than she could bear, and she sank down beside him with a little cry.

Cyrano pushed away every helping hand and rose unsteadily from the bench, and then, with a sound like a trumpet, he drew his sword from its scabbard. He declared that he would not die in a chair or in a bed, but on his feet with his blade in his hand, as a man of his sort ought to do. His old enemy, he added, was coming for him, and he meant to meet it.

Swaying on his feet, Cyrano fought the shadows in the empty air, lunging and parrying and crying out the names of his oldest enemies one by one. There was Falsehood, and Compromise, and Prejudice, and a dozen more, and he struck at each of them in turn with all the grace that he had shown on the night of the Porte de Nesle. The sisters watched from the cloister in awed silence, and none of them dared to go forward or to speak a single word.

Cyrano cried that Cowardice and Folly should never defeat him either, for he had not yielded to them in all his life and would not begin tonight. He lunged again, and again, and his sword flashed in the darkness like a silver fish in a pool, while Le Bret held out his arms and Ragueneau wept openly. The garden rang with the sound of a battle that only he could see.

At length he leaned against the trunk of the great tree, gasping for breath, with the sword still held out before him like a challenge. He said that he knew very well who would strike him down in the end, and that it was useless to fight such an enemy, but that a man did not fight only to win. The more hopeless the battle, he said, the finer it was, and the prouder a man ought to be to fight it to the end.

Roxane threw her arms around him and begged him to live, crying that she loved him, that she had always loved him and that she could not bear to lose him now. Cyrano answered very gently that it was too late, and that the only thing he had ever asked from any woman was a little kindness, which he had been given at last, on this last evening. It was more than he had ever dared to hope for in all his years of walking alone through the world.

With a twinkle in his eye Cyrano remarked to Le Bret that the playwright Molière had borrowed a scene from one of his comedies, and had made a great success of it. Molière had genius, he said, and Christian had been handsome, and for his own part he had been given a great deal of wit and a very great nose. He laughed at his own joke with all his old mischief, and his friend, who loved him dearly, could only weep.

As the pale moon rose over the convent wall, Cyrano raised his eyes to it and smiled the smile of a man who has found an old friend. He said that he was going there at last, since he had always said that he had fallen from it, and that he would find Socrates and Galileo waiting to talk with him. He did not seem in the least afraid of the journey, and his face in the moonlight was as calm as a child's.

Cyrano drew himself up against the tree, though his strength was nearly gone, and said that Death might take his laurels and his roses, and everything else that the world had ever given him. But there was one thing, he said in a ringing voice, that it could never take, and that he would carry with him whether it liked it or not. The garden was very still, and the sisters in the cloister held their breath and waited for his answer.

He said it at last, in a voice that was almost a whisper, and yet that seemed to fill the whole garden: the thing he would take with him, without a crease or a stain, was his panache. Roxane bent down, with tears pouring down her face, and kissed his forehead, and Cyrano smiled and his eyes shone in the moonlight. It was a small and quiet kiss, and it was all that he had ever wished for.

Cyrano's strength failed at last, and he sank down into Roxane's arms and died there in the quiet garden, with the autumn leaves falling softly around them. He had lived without ever bending his head, he had loved without ever asking for return, and he had gone out of the world as proud and brave and witty as he had come into it. Roxane held him close and wept, and his spirit seemed to remain behind in the gathering dusk like a white plume that no wind could blow away.
